question: How can concrete construction become circular?

answer.answer:
Making concrete work circular runs through one route in the cited literature: design the structure for disassembly with reversible connections rather than glued or monolithic joints (VA15), and underpin it with component-level traceable data, material passports in effect (VA9), which is what makes recovery and reuse economically worth doing. What it buys is material and energy saving and reduced CO2 and waste (VA4), and the data layer separately takes the edge off cost and investment uncertainty (RI3). Both links are thinly exhibited: of the 50 coded cases, 5 carry the data-to-circularity link and 6 the circularity-to-saving link, and circular construction is drawn on by only 8 of the 50 while traceable data is drawn on by 26, so the data infrastructure is common and the circular design intent that should sit on top of it is rare. No deployed project record appears in the material in front of me, and the only concrete-specific requirement visible is certification of 3D printed concrete walls, which makes regulatory approval (RI18) a precondition of additive manufacturing (PR3).

**The one cited path in and out of circularity**

VA15 "Circular construction/DfDisAssembly" (Value) carries exactly one inbound and one outbound dependency edge, and both are listed, so this is the complete cited connection for it, not a sample. Upstream, VA9 "Allow traceable/linked data" enables VA15, on the mechanism that component data and material passports make recovery and reuse economically viable [1] (DEP69, peer-reviewed, carried by 5 of the 50). Downstream, VA15 enables VA4 "Material/energy saving/reduce CO2/waste", on the mechanism that glued and monolithic joints limit salvage potential while reversible connection design under DfDisAssembly enables material recovery [2] (DEP52, peer-reviewed, carried by 6 of the 50). That mechanism is the practical instruction for concrete specifically: monolithic and adhesive jointing is what forecloses salvage, so the design decision that matters is the connection detail.

The asymmetry across this path is worth stating. 26 of the 50 coded cases draw on VA9 "Allow traceable/linked data" [3], 8 draw on VA15 "Circular construction/DfDisAssembly" [3], and 15 draw on VA4 "Material/energy saving/reduce CO2/waste" [3]. The tracked-data precondition is already widespread; the circular design intent is not.

**A second return on the same data layer**

VA9 also mitigates RI3 "Increase cost/investment uncertainty", on the grounds that material passports reduce uncertainty about the circular potential and economics of disassembled elements [3] (DEP70, peer-reviewed, carried by 7 of the 50), with 13 of the 50 cases drawing on RI3 [3]. So the investment in traceability pays twice, once toward circularity and once against the cost uncertainty that usually blocks it.

**What sits alongside circularity in practice, as correlation only**

The co-occurrence profile for VA15 is statistical, not a dependency claim, and the list is a cut rather than a total: the strongest correlates are PR10 "Material testing" (weight 8), VA14 "Integrate supply chain" (7), PR5 "Modularisation" (6), CO11 "Early contractor involvement" (6), PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" (6), RI3 (6), AC3 "Design engineer" (5), AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" (5), PR7 "Subtractive manufacturing" (4), RE7 "CNC machines" (4) and RI16 "Increase material usage/waste" (3), out of 125 co-occurring enablers in total [4]. Read as a pattern of company, not causation: circular work in this record tends to appear where material testing, an integrated supply chain and early contractor involvement are already present.

**The regulatory gate on concrete**

Where the concrete is printed rather than cast or precast, approval is the binding constraint. PR3 "Additive manufacturing" depends on RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", because 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability [5] (DEP83, resting on a standard, carried by 2 of the 50), and on-site DFAB (PR8) likewise depends on RI18, via an alternative-means approval pathway [3] (DEP84, carried by 2 of the 50). 12 of the 50 coded cases draw on RI18 [3]. The context does not connect RI18 to VA15, so nothing here tells you how a disassembly-designed concrete element would be certified.

**Limits of this answer**

The retrieved material contains no enabler labelled for concrete work as such, so everything above is the general circularity path applied to concrete, plus the two concrete-printing certification edges; it does not establish what the record holds on cast or precast concrete specifically. And there is no deployed process record, firm or census entry in front of me for circular concrete, so this rests on the cited literature and on how many of the 50 coded cases carry each link, not on a named deployment.
